newsitem.title: USA: Exiles hold peaceful demonstration off Cuban coast.
newsitem.headline: Exiles hold peaceful demonstration off Cuban coast.

text.p: Cuban exiles held a peaceful demonstration off Cuba's north coast on Saturday to promote a national work stoppage on the Communist-ruled Caribbean island, the U.S. Coast Guard said.

A flotilla of about 10 vessels, far fewer than the exile group Democracy Movement had intended, gathered near Cuba's 12-mile territorial waters limit off Havana, where crewmembers held a prayer service, Coast Guard spokesman Scott Carr said.
"We haven't heard any reports of trouble," Carr said. "They're heading back."

The flotilla was the first of three scheduled for this year, leading up to Pope John Paul's visit to Cuba in early 1998. It was the latest in a series of flotillas mounted by Miami-based Cuban exiles that have served to heighten tension between the United States and Fidel Castro's Communist regime.
Cuba on Thursday described the flotilla as a "new attempt at a provocation" and said it would use "the necessary means" to ensure there were no violations of its territory.
Democracy Movement had assured U.S. and Cuban authorities it did not intend to enter Cuban waters.
Organizers said at least three dozen vessels headed to the limit of Cuban territorial waters in two groups that left late on Friday and early on Saturday from the Florida Keys.
About a dozen aircraft were to join them. But rough seas and heavy thunderstorms forced some of the boats to abandon the trip and the planes never took off, the Coast Guard said.

"They ran into a little weather problem," Carr said. "The planes aren't flying." He said there were no reports that any Cuban military vessel or aircraft had been seen at the site of the demonstration.

Miami-based Cuban exiles have sent a number of flotillas across the Florida Straits between Florida and Cuba. During one in 1995, a Democracy Movement boat entered Cuban waters and was sideswiped by Cuban military vessels.
In February 1996, Cuban MiG fighter jets shot down two unarmed U.S. civilian planes between Florida and Cuba, killing four aviators of the exile group Brothers to the Rescue.

The incident provoked international outrage against Cuba. But President Fidel Castro's government defended its action by saying the planes were violating its territory. Washington said the downed planes were outside Cuban airspace and should not have been shot down.

Democracy Movement said Saturday's flotilla was aimed at publicizing within Cuba the idea of a general strike at an as- yet-undetermined date. The group espouses nonviolent protest with the aim of stirring democratic reforms in Cuba.
Democracy Movement leaders have said they reserve their right as Cuban citizens to enter Cuban territory at any time and intend to exercise that right during the pope's visit.
